strengths: Originality: Using attention-dependent heteroscedastic GP smoothing to construct multiple CDE control paths is a useful architectural combination. Targeting control-path construction offers a complementary approach to improving the vector field or solver.

Significance: Table 1 reports substantial improvements over the evaluated spline CDEs. MVC-GP achieves accuracies of 95.07%, 98.28%, and 95.39% across the three datasets, alongside markedly lower NFE and total runtime.

Experimental merits: The evaluation includes five seeds, single-path smoothing baselines, head-count and bandwidth ablations, solver-tolerance comparisons, and noise perturbations. Figure 4 supports the empirical claim that smoothing reduces sensitivity of solver cost to added noise.

Presentation and reproducibility: The architecture and weighted-path equations are understandable, and Appendix B supplies hardware, optimizer settings, preprocessing, and several hyperparameter ranges. Training-only normalization is appropriate. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for these benchmark experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—central complexity theorem is incorrect as stated. Appendix A.1 asserts that boundedness and Lipschitz continuity of the vector field imply that higher solution derivatives are proportional to the corresponding control derivatives. The chain rule instead introduces products involving lower control derivatives and derivatives of the vector field. For example, X(t)=t and f(z)=tanh(z), with a nonzero initial state, produce a nonlinear solution with nonzero higher derivatives although X^(p+1)=0. Thus Theorem 3.1 cannot strictly determine NFE from the proposed control-path integral. The spline complexity formulas are also not derived from that integral. High-frequency forcing and numerical stiffness are repeatedly conflated without a stability analysis.

Soundness—the smoothing and multi-head results are also unsupported. Appendix A.3 applies a convolution derivative argument to normalized Nadaraya–Watson regression and GP regression without accounting for the normalization denominator or the coefficients (K+Σ)^(-1)X. Bounds require additional dependence on sampling geometry, noise regularization, or conditioning. Moreover, an upper derivative bound cannot establish NFE proportionality. Theorem 3.4 therefore does not follow: the smallest bandwidth need not dominate if its head has negligible dynamics. Appendix A.5 establishes GP optimality only under the assumed generative prior, not general reconstruction superiority or optimality of the data-dependent attentive estimator.

Efficiency accounting contains a consequential ambiguity. Sections 3.4 and C.4 describe GP fitting as a static, one-time preprocessing cost. However, Equation (4) uses a noise matrix determined by trainable, input-dependent attention. Updating the attention changes the linear system, requiring recomputation during training unless an additional approximation or freezing procedure is used. The manuscript does not reconcile this with its timing breakdown. End-to-end timing should explicitly include these solves and differentiation through them. The headline inference-efficiency claim is also not directly established by Table 1's metric, which combines fitting, training, and one test pass.

The evaluation does not adequately isolate the architectural contribution. Each head has its own vector field and hidden state, and MVC adds a CNN, but parameter counts and capacity-matched comparisons are absent. A CNN/attention classifier without CDE integration, and a matched multi-head spline model, would help establish whether attentive smoothing is responsible for the accuracy gains. Using identical short training schedules for spline baselines does not establish comparable convergence or optimal tuning.

Significance is overstated relative to the evidence. Experiments cover only three short, regularly sampled classification datasets, with fresh 60/20/20 splits rather than the archive's standard evaluation protocol. These results support improvements over the reported implementations, not the repeated state-of-the-art claim. Irregular sampling, missing observations, and long-sequence scaling are not evaluated despite motivating the method. GRU-D is faster on every dataset in Table 1, so the efficiency advantage needs qualification.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The paper does not clearly specify whether bandwidths are fixed, tuned, or learned; how head outputs are combined; the numerical stabilization used for GP solves; or the handling of padding in attention and smoothing. Appendix B.2's claim that repeated-value padding yields zero derivatives does not generally hold for globally smoothed GP/kernel paths. No implementation link is provided, and Appendix B.6 specifies a UWave cubic tolerance that differs from Table 1.

Presentation and limitations need tighter calibration. Appendix C.3 argues that heterogeneous bandwidths provide the better trade-off, yet the primary models use homogeneous bandwidths on two datasets; this discrepancy is not explained. The discussion should acknowledge the offline nature of globally conditioned paths and full-sequence attention, the untested cubic GP scaling, and the distinction between improved classification and demonstrated recovery of high-frequency information. The useful empirical idea merits further development, but the central theoretical errors and unresolved computational accounting prevent acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Reducing adaptive-solver cost through control-path smoothing addresses a useful practical bottleneck in Neural CDEs. The reported results warrant further investigation: Table 1 gives MVC-GP accuracies of 95.07%, 98.28%, and 95.39%, with substantial runtime improvements over the evaluated spline CDEs.

Originality: Combining attention-dependent observation noise, multiple GP control paths, and jointly integrated CDE heads is an interesting architectural contribution. Using attention to select which observations smoothing should preserve provides a concrete mechanism beyond simply increasing bandwidth.

Empirical evidence: The evaluation includes five seeds, single-path smoothing baselines, bandwidth and head-count ablations, solver-tolerance sweeps, and noise perturbations. Figure 4 supports the narrower empirical claim that smoothing reduces sensitivity of NFE to the tested additive noise.

Presentation and reproducibility: The main architecture is understandable, and Appendix B provides hardware, optimizer, preprocessing, and several hyperparameter details. Training-only normalization and validation checkpointing are appropriate. The benchmark-based study raises no evident material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—central NFE theory is incorrect as stated. Theorem 3.1 and Appendix A.1 assert that higher solution derivatives scale proportionally to the corresponding control-path derivative under a bounded, Lipschitz vector field. Differentiating the CDE introduces derivatives and products involving the vector field and lower-order control derivatives. For example, X(t)=t has vanishing higher derivatives, yet a bounded nonlinear field such as f(z)=2+sin(z) generally produces a solution with nonzero higher derivatives and numerical integration error. Thus NFE is not strictly determined by the proposed control-path quantity. The spline complexity formulas are also asserted without a valid derivation, and high NFE alone does not establish numerical stiffness.

Soundness—the smoothing and multi-head guarantees do not follow. Theorem 3.2 applies a convolution-style bound to normalized Nadaraya–Watson regression and GP posterior means without controlling the normalization denominator or GP inverse coefficients. For two observations with values -1 and 1 separated by D, the normalized Gaussian smoother has midpoint slope D/(2h²), contradicting the stated universal first-derivative bound proportional to 1/h. GP bounds likewise require additional dependence on conditioning, noise, and sampling. Corollary 3.3 then turns an upper bound into a proportionality, and Theorem 3.4 incorrectly makes the smallest bandwidth alone determine NFE, regardless of head dynamics or amplitude. These are central claims requiring substantial correction.

Efficiency accounting is unresolved. Sections 3.4 and C.4 describe GP fitting as a one-time preprocessing cost, but the weighted GP covariance in Equation (4) depends on learned attention scores and therefore changes during training. Its factorization cannot generally be precomputed once. The implementation must explain which computations are cached, which are differentiated, and where repeated solves are timed. Table 1 reports combined fitting, training, and testing time; Figure 10 provides only a coarse inference breakdown. This is insufficient to substantiate the abstract's inference-speed claim or broader scalability claims without sequence-length and head-count scaling measurements.

Evaluation scope and comparison fairness limit significance. All three experiments use regularly spaced sequences; there is no missingness or irregular-sampling evaluation despite this being a major motivation. The custom 60/20/20 splits and limited baseline set do not establish state-of-the-art performance on these benchmarks. Spline baselines receive the proposed methods' short training schedules and learning rates rather than independently optimized schedules, leaving convergence fairness uncertain. GRU-D is also faster than MVC-GP on every dataset, so the efficiency advantage needs to be stated relative to the relevant CDE baselines.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed explanation for the gains. Multiple independent vector fields and a CNN add capacity, but parameter counts and capacity-matched controls are absent. Useful controls include multiple paths without learned attention, a comparable CNN-attention classifier without CDE integration, and an equally sized single-path model. Attention heatmaps and improved classification do not demonstrate recovery of high-frequency information. Moreover, the best MVC-GP models on two datasets use identical bandwidths across heads, limiting the evidence that scale diversity is the decisive mechanism.

Reproducibility has material gaps and inconsistencies. The manuscript does not provide code or fully specify the differentiation strategy, multi-head initialization and readout, numerical stabilization, or whether bandwidths are fixed or learned. Appendix B.2 claims repeated-value padding produces zero derivatives in padded regions, which does not generally hold for the global RBF smoothers. Appendix B.6 specifies a UWave solver tolerance of 10^-4 for cubic CDEs, whereas Table 1 reports 10^-3. These details affect both accuracy and runtime.

Limitations and claim calibration need improvement. Appendix A.5 establishes GP reconstruction optimality under the assumed GP/noise model, not unconditional superiority on real signals or downstream classification. The paper does not adequately discuss this assumption, full-sequence access, cubic GP scaling, or the narrow benchmark coverage. Although the architecture and empirical gains have merit, the invalid theoretical guarantees and unresolved evaluation/accounting issues prevent acceptance in the present form.

strengths: Significance: Smoothing the driving path addresses a practical bottleneck in Neural CDEs. Table 1 reports substantial improvements over the evaluated spline baselines: MVC-GP achieves 95.07%, 98.28%, and 95.39% accuracy across the three datasets, with considerably lower runtime and NFE.

Originality: Combining attention-dependent GP observation noise with multiple jointly integrated CDE paths is a useful architectural contribution. The convolutional extension provides a plausible mechanism for preserving task-relevant local information under strong smoothing.

Empirical evidence: The evaluation includes five seeds, single-path smoothing baselines, head-count and bandwidth ablations, solver-tolerance comparisons, and test-time noise experiments. Figure 4 supports improved robustness of both accuracy and solver cost to additive noise.

Presentation and reproducibility: The pipeline diagrams and explicit path-construction equations make the method understandable. Appendix B provides hardware, preprocessing, optimization settings, and hyperparameter ranges. Training-only normalization and validation-based checkpoint selection are appropriate. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central solver theorem: Theorem 3.1 and Appendix A.1 incorrectly infer that higher derivatives of the solution are proportional to the corresponding derivatives of the control from boundedness and Lipschitz continuity of the vector field. For example, X(t)=t has vanishing higher derivatives, but z'=tanh(z) generally does not. Conversely, a zero vector field makes control roughness irrelevant. Thus NFE is not strictly determined by the stated control-path integral, and the subsequent spline complexity formulas are not established. Rapidly varying forcing also does not by itself establish numerical stiffness.

Soundness—smoothing bounds: Theorem 3.2 applies a convolution bound to normalized Nadaraya–Watson regression and GP posterior means without controlling the normalization or inverse Gram matrix. GP derivative bounds generally involve the coefficients (K+Sigma)^{-1}X and hence conditioning, noise, and observation geometry. Moreover, an upper bound cannot establish the proportionality NFE ∝ h^{-1}. The strict minimum-bandwidth law in Theorem 3.4 inherits these problems and ignores head-specific amplitudes and vector fields.

Efficiency and reproducibility: The claim that GP inversion is a one-time preprocessing cost conflicts with Equation (4): Sigma depends on attention scores produced by trainable queries and convolutional features, so the matrix changes during training and across samples. The manuscript does not explain how these changing systems are solved, differentiated through, or included in runtime measurements. This ambiguity directly affects the main efficiency claim.

Evaluation fairness: Appendix B fixes spline baselines to the proposed models' learning rates and short training schedules rather than demonstrating that each baseline is adequately optimized. Multiple heads also introduce separate vector fields and additional capacity, without parameter-matched controls. A CNN/attention classifier without CDE integration and a comparably equipped spline CDE are needed to isolate the contribution of attentive smoothing.

Significance and claim scope: Three short, regularly sampled classification datasets do not establish broad scalability or effectiveness on irregular and missing observations. The experiments use new 60/20/20 splits and a limited baseline set, so they support superiority among the tested configurations rather than state-of-the-art accuracy. GRU-D is faster on all three datasets, and the principal timing metric combines fitting, training, and testing rather than directly establishing the abstract's inference-speed claim.

Limitations and precision: Appendix A.5 establishes GP optimality only under the assumed GP data-generating model; it does not guarantee better reconstruction of arbitrary signals. The manuscript does not adequately discuss this restriction, the noncausal use of complete sequences, or the scaling of dynamic GP solves. Implementation details also need reconciliation: Appendix B.6 specifies UWave spline tolerance 10^{-4}, whereas Table 1 lists 10^{-3} for Cubic, and constant-value padding does not generally imply exactly zero derivatives for globally smoothed paths.

strengths: Significance: Reducing adaptive-solver cost through task-aware control-path smoothing addresses a practical bottleneck in Neural CDEs. The reported gains are substantial: on UWaveGestureLibrary, Table 2 improves accuracy from 85.68% for cubic CDE to 95.39% for MVC-GP while reducing total time from 81.78 to 12.29 seconds.

Originality: Using learned attention scores as heteroscedastic GP observation precisions is an interesting architectural contribution. Combining this construction with multiple jointly integrated paths provides a plausible way to balance smoothing and predictive expressivity.

Empirical coverage: The paper includes five-seed results, approximately parameter-matched principal CDE baselines, solver-tolerance sweeps, noise and missingness experiments, and ablations of smoothing, attention, convolution, head count, and solver choice. These provide useful evidence beyond the three primary classification benchmarks.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture is explained clearly through equations and pipeline figures. The discussion candidly acknowledges bandwidth tuning, adaptive-solver dependence, and possible loss of predictive high-frequency information. Public benchmark use presents no evident material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—central NFE theorem is false as stated. Appendix A.1 assumes that bounded, Lipschitz f implies that the solution's higher derivatives are proportional to the corresponding control-path derivative. Nonlinear chain-rule terms invalidate this: with X(t)=t and f(z)=tanh(z), X^(p+1)=0 for p>=1, yet a nonconstant solution has nonzero higher derivatives and requires numerical integration. Theorem 3.1 therefore bounds positive NFE by zero. Moreover, an upper constraint on acceptable step size does not establish the claimed upper bound on NFE, especially including rejected steps. The spline complexity formulas and Theorem 3.4 inherit these problems. Path roughness can increase integration cost, but the manuscript does not establish numerical stiffness as its primary cause.

Soundness—smoothing guarantees omit essential dependencies. Theorem 3.2 treats normalized discrete kernel regression and GP posterior means as ordinary convolution smoothers. Nadaraya–Watson differentiation involves the normalization denominator and sampling geometry; GP derivatives depend on coefficients (K+Sigma)^(-1)X and hence conditioning, noise, and observation configuration. A constant depending only on kernel shape is not justified. Consequently, the claimed bandwidth-only NFE scaling and independence from input noise are unsupported. Appendix A.5 establishes GP optimality only under the assumed correctly specified probabilistic model, not generally superior reconstruction of real signals.

Efficiency and reproducibility: Sections 3.4 and C.3 describe GP fitting as one-time preprocessing, but the proposed attention-dependent Sigma changes as the queries and CNN are trained. Its factorization generally must be recomputed for each updated forward pass. The paper needs to explain exactly what is cached, what is differentiated, and whether repeated fitting is included in training timings. Additionally, Table 3 reports 62,324 MB peak GPU memory for Mamba, inconsistent with the stated single NVIDIA L40 setup, whose memory capacity is 48 GB. The separate H100 profiling does not explain this table. These inconsistencies undermine the central computational comparison.

Evaluation fairness and attribution: Linear and cubic CDEs receive the proposed method's fixed learning rates and short training schedules rather than independent optimization; sharing these settings does not establish a fair accuracy–time frontier. The smoothing-spline baseline uses one fixed penalty, whereas the proposed smoothers receive a broad bandwidth search, and Table 10 omits its timing and NFE. A matched CNN/attention pooling baseline and a CNN-augmented spline CDE would help determine how much improvement comes from smoothing and continuous integration versus the added feature extractor.

Data protocol and reproducibility: Appendix B specifies 60/20/20 partitions for every dataset without explaining whether ETTm1 is split chronologically before windowing. Randomly splitting overlapping forecasting windows could leak closely related observations across partitions; the causal boundary within each individual window does not resolve this concern. Exact split construction, selected hidden dimensions, padding masks, differentiation strategy, and whether bandwidths are fixed or learned also need clarification. In particular, repeating the final observation does not generally produce zero derivative throughout padded regions for globally fitted GP or kernel paths, contrary to the preprocessing description.

Significance and claim calibration: The claim of consistently achieving state-of-the-art accuracy is unsupported by the selected baselines and contradicted within Table 2 on CharacterTrajectories, where Mamba achieves 96.64% versus MVC-GP's 95.07%. Custom archive splits further limit comparison with established benchmark results. The short-window forecasting experiment supports causal windowed prediction, but does not demonstrate scalable streaming latency or long-sequence efficiency for repeated cubic-cost GP fitting. The empirical idea remains promising, but the incorrect theoretical foundation and unresolved efficiency accounting require substantial revision before acceptance.

strengths: Originality: Combining attention-dependent kernel/GP smoothing with jointly integrated multi-view CDEs is a useful architectural idea. Learning which observations to preserve addresses a practical tension between smoothing and predictive information.

Significance: The reported improvements over spline CDEs are substantial. On UWaveGestureLibrary, MVC-GP achieves 95.39% accuracy versus 85.68% for cubic CDEs, with reported total time decreasing from 81.78 to 12.29 seconds (Table 2). Such gains would be valuable for continuous-time sequence modeling if independently reproduced.

Evaluation: The paper includes five-seed results, approximately parameter-matched principal CDE comparisons, noise and missingness experiments, and ablations covering attention, convolution, bandwidth, head count, and solver choice. The supplementary forecasting and high-dimensional experiments broaden the evidence.

Presentation and limitations: The main architectural equations are understandable, and the paper explicitly discusses bandwidth tuning, loss of high-frequency information, and window-level causality. Appendix B supplies substantial optimization details and training-only normalization. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—Theorem 3.1 is false as stated. Appendix A.1 asserts that solution derivatives are proportional to corresponding control-path derivatives for bounded Lipschitz vector fields. The chain rule also produces terms involving derivatives of the vector field and lower-order control derivatives. For example, X(t)=t and f(z)=2+sin(z) satisfy these assumptions, yet the solution has nonzero higher derivatives while X^(p+1)=0; the proposed NFE upper bound is therefore zero for a nontrivial integration. Moreover, an upper constraint on step size does not establish the claimed upper bound on step count, and rejected steps are not controlled. These problems undermine a central theoretical contribution and its corollaries.

Soundness—Theorem 3.2 is not established for the stated estimators. Appendix A.3 treats normalized discrete Nadaraya–Watson regression and GP posterior means as simple kernel convolutions. For Nadaraya–Watson regression, derivatives depend on the normalization denominator and sampling geometry; for GPs, they depend on coefficients involving (K+Σ)^(-1), hence conditioning and noise regularization. These dependencies cannot generally be absorbed into a constant depending solely on kernel shape. Consequently, the claimed noise/grid-independent NFE scaling and the multi-head bound in Theorem 3.4 are unsupported. Path roughness also does not by itself establish numerical stiffness in its conventional sense.

Computational accounting: Section 3.4 and Appendix C.3 describe GP fitting as a static, one-time preprocessing cost. However, the main method uses Σ determined by trainable attention scores (Equation 4), so its GP solve generally changes with every parameter update and input. Kernel matrices may be cached, but the attention-dependent factorization cannot simply be precomputed once. The paper needs to explain how repeated solves and their gradients enter training timings. Without this, the central efficiency interpretation is difficult to verify.

Evaluation validity: The claim of consistently achieving state-of-the-art accuracy is contradicted by Table 2: Mamba reaches 96.64% on CharacterTrajectories versus MVC-GP's 95.07%. The custom 60/20/20 splits also do not establish state of the art on standard benchmark protocols. For ETTm1, Appendix B applies this general splitting description without specifying chronological boundaries or whether overlapping windows are separated before splitting; the forecasting evaluation therefore leaves potential leakage unresolved.

Baseline fairness and attribution: Spline CDEs receive the proposed methods' learning rates and short training schedules rather than independently optimized schedules. The smoothing-spline comparison fixes α=0.5 and reports accuracy without its runtime/NFE trade-off. There is also no matched convolution-plus-attention classifier without CDE integration, or equivalent convolutional front end for spline baselines. Thus, the experiments do not sufficiently isolate the contribution of attentive GP path construction from additional feature extraction and optimization choices.

Reproducibility and reporting: Table 3 reports approximately 62 GB of Mamba peak memory on SpokenArabicDigits, whereas Appendix B.3 says all models were trained on a single L40, which has 48 GB. Appendix C.3 separately uses an H100 with unspecified small batch sizes. Hardware, implementation, memory measurement, and timing protocols need reconciliation before the strong memory and latency conclusions are reliable. Important implementation details also remain unclear, including missing-observation handling and whether bandwidths are fixed or learned.

Claim calibration: Appendix A.5 establishes GP optimality only under its assumed prior and observation model, not generally for real signals or the data-dependent attentive estimator. Similarly, qualitative attention maps and classification gains do not demonstrate recovery of discarded high-frequency information. The promising empirical method remains a discernible contribution, but unsupported central theory and unresolved evaluation/accounting issues prevent acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Reducing adaptive-solver cost through task-aware control-path smoothing addresses a useful bottleneck in Neural CDEs. The reported improvements are substantial: on UWaveGestureLibrary, MVC GP achieves 95.39% accuracy versus 85.68% for cubic CDEs, with total time decreasing from 81.78 to 12.29 seconds (Table 2).

Originality: Combining attention-dependent observation noise, multiple GP control paths, and joint CDE integration is a meaningful architectural contribution, even though the individual components are established.

Evaluation: The manuscript includes five-seed results, approximately parameter-matched CDE baselines, tolerance sweeps, and supplementary experiments on missingness, noise, solver choice, and high-dimensional inputs. These provide useful empirical evidence beyond the primary classification benchmarks.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline and weighted-path equations are understandable. The discussion appropriately acknowledges bandwidth sensitivity, information loss, and the shared solver’s bottleneck. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central NFE theorem is invalid as stated. Appendix A.1 assumes that higher solution derivatives scale linearly with the corresponding control derivative. Differentiating z'=f(z)X' also produces terms involving derivatives of f and products of lower-order derivatives of X. For example, X(t)=t and bounded Lipschitz f(z)=2+sin(z) produce nonlinear solution dynamics although X^(p+1)=0, making Theorem 3.1’s proposed upper bound zero. The proof also converts an upper bound on step size into an upper bound on inverse step size in the wrong direction and does not bound rejected steps. Consequently, the spline estimates, Corollary 3.3, and Theorem 3.4 lack their claimed foundation. Rapidly varying forcing is also repeatedly conflated with numerical stiffness without establishing stiffness.

Soundness—Theorem 3.2 applies a convolution bound to different estimators without justification. Nadaraya–Watson regression has a time-dependent denominator whose derivatives matter; the GP mean contains coefficients (K+Σ)^(-1)X whose size depends on conditioning, observation noise, and sampling geometry. Neither is controlled by a kernel-shape-only constant as claimed. Attention-dependent weighting requires further analysis. Appendix A.5 establishes GP optimality only under the assumed probabilistic model, not general superiority on real signals or downstream tasks.

Efficiency and reproducibility: Section 3.4 and Appendix C.3 describe GP fitting as one-time preprocessing, but the proposed GP covariance Σ depends on learned attention scores and therefore changes during training. The manuscript must explain which quantities are cached and account for repeated solves and their gradients. The H100 timing breakdown also uses unspecified small batches, unlike the main L40 setup. Table 3 reports approximately 62 GB of peak GPU memory for Mamba despite the stated single-L40 training setup, requiring reconciliation before accepting the memory comparison.

Evaluation and significance: The claim that MVC GP consistently achieves state-of-the-art accuracy contradicts Table 2, where Mamba scores 96.64% versus MVC GP’s 95.07% on CharacterTrajectories. Custom 60/20/20 splits also prevent direct comparison with established benchmark results. Shared short training schedules do not establish that spline baselines are adequately optimized, and the smoothing-spline baseline uses a single fixed penalty without reporting its efficiency. A matched CNN/attention model without CDE integration would help establish the value added by the continuous-time component.

Reproducibility: The manuscript does not provide code or sufficiently complete configurations to resolve important implementation questions, including whether bandwidths are learned or fixed, padding masks during smoothing and attention, and missing-observation handling. For ETTm1, the generic split description does not establish chronological separation or explain how overlapping windows are kept from crossing splits; causal construction within each window alone does not resolve that evaluation concern.

Presentation: Several interpretations exceed the evidence. Attention plots do not establish recovery of high-frequency information, and aggregate training timings do not establish low-latency streaming performance. The strong empirical promise merits further development, but the incorrect central theorems and unresolved computational accounting prevent acceptance in the present form.
